utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon. You can hear it?

utterances.speaker: MR. BALIJAGIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you kindly call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-01-48-PT, the Prosecutor versus Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: May I have the appearances.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. Good afternoon --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: I apologise. Good afternoon, Your Honour, good afternoon, counsel. For the Prosecution appear Mr. Carl Koenig on my right-hand side, trial attorney, Mr. David Le. The case manager on my left-hand side, and myself Ekkehard Whitopf, Senior Trial Attorney.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Whitopf. And for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. BALIJAGIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. My name is Faruk Balijagic. I am the Defence counsel for Mr. Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Balijagic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BALIJAGIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, the first Status Conference took place on January 8th, if I'm correct, and this is the second Status Conference. I think there are several matters to be considered during this conference, one of which will be the Prosecution's motion regarding the application for the extension of time. But before we get to that matter, I'd like to firstly deal with the issue of Defence counsel. I heard, Mr. Balijagic, that you were planning to withdraw from the case due to your illness and to have co-counsel, and I noticed that a legal assistant has been -- was assigned to you last month. So I'd like to hear from you what your current position is. Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BALIJAGIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to thank the Registry. I was assigned a legal assistant three or four days ago. It is Dijana Kreho an attorney. I would like to familiarise her with the case. In the previous meetings with Ms. Featherstone, we did broach this issue, but it will not affect the course of the proceedings as I will inform you in more detail in my later pleadings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you also make any comments on the matter of co-counsel --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Could you make any comments on the matter of co-counsel as you said previously, or have you applied for the assignment of co-counsel yet?

utterances.speaker: MR. BALIJAGIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Dijana Kreho has already been appointed, and she is in fact getting familiar with the case and will soon be ready to -- will know everything that there is to know about the indictment and the Defence moves so far. So I would like to assure you that there will be no delays in the proceedings because of this. And I am also duty-bound to let you know that 15 days ago I submitted a motion to Chief Prosecutor Carla Del Ponte containing 49 pages, with a number of documents containing some facts which can be verified and this is all in support of our motion to withdraw charges against Sefer Halilovic. The Chief Prosecutor has not yet received this motion, but she will be considering it in due time. Do I have to make any other clarifications?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, those kinds of matters regarding substance, substantial matter, will be dealt with separately, and the main purpose of this pre-trial procedure is to deal with some procedural matters and to make the case get ready for the trial. So that will be dealt with later on. But could you make comment, did I hear about the resignation of yourself? I'm clarifying to you whether you are going to resign or not, because I heard that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BALIJAGIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No. I am not going to resign. I simply said that I need an assistant or co-counsel to be assigned to me because if my illness progresses, that would make it possible for me to withdraw at that stage and that person could then replace me. And according to what I can say right now, it seems likely that I will withdraw from the case, but I have to abide by the wishes of my client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. There might have been some misunderstanding. Thank you, Mr. Balijagic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BALIJAGIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Okay. I remained seized of the Prosecution's motion. I have them in front of me, the motion of 28th of March in which the Prosecution has requested an extension of time to file a pre-trial brief due to reasons of untranslated materials and the belated date that an expert report can be produced. However, it is my understanding also that the Prosecution is able to submit a pre-trial brief at the end of this month, but it would like to have this one as a provisional one with the final brief being submitted in September. In this regard, I'd like to hear your submissions, but please bear in mind that I have the written motion already. So please make it as brief as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will make it as brief as possible. At the latest Status Conference held on 8 January, Your Honour ordered the Prosecution to file its pre-trial brief by 29th of April, 2000. The Defence was ordered to file its pre-trial brief on 31st July, 2002. Since the last Status Conference, a number of issues have arisen that have serious impact on the further proceedings, especially on the further schedule. Those developments have intensively been discussed with the officer on the Rule 65 ter meetings and I am aware that you have been comprehensively been briefed about these meetings. All of these developments and especially impact on the schedule on the future proceedings were not foreseeable prior to the last Status Conference in January 2002. Some of them are actually caused by the Defence and you addressed one of them, especially since my learned colleague, Mr. Balijagic, on the Defence side has chosen to withdraw from the Defence. There are a number of issues I would like to address. The first is the withdrawal of Mr. Balijagic as Defence counsel. The second one is a jurisdictional issue that has been arisen in the Hadzihasanovic and others case, and that will play a crucial role in this case as well. The issue of stipulation would be the third issue I would like to address, and again we will address the issue of translations, the usual bottleneck of ICTY proceedings and finally the issue of the military expert. I very much appreciate that you, Your Honour, already have addressed the issue of a potential or a likely withdrawal of Mr. Balijagic from his position as a Defence counsel for Mr. Halilovic, the accused. And again, what he told us today is confusing, and it's not the first time confusing. I will give you a brief summary what happened. Mr. Balijagic, on the occasion of the Rule 65 ter meeting in February this year, for the first time announced that he would withdraw from the Defence due to health problems. He repeated this announcement on 21st of March on the occasion of the last Rule 65 ter meeting. In February, Mr. Balijagic stressed that he would get an assistant soon. In March, meaning 21st March 2002, but however, Mr. Balijagic had not yet a co-counsel assign. He then announced that his client, the accused would like to hire an US attorney. Again today in a meeting we had with Mr. Balijagic a few hours ago, he corroborated as he did in front of you his announcement to resign without being specific as to the date when this will happen. He announced, however, at least to us that this will happen very soon, in the next future. According to him, and this has been corroborated now, he got an assistant signed only three to four days ago. Mr. Balijagic is still not in a position to clarify as to whether this further lawyer would take over as a Defence lead counsel after he has withdrawn. That means we know that there will be a change in the person of the Defence counsel in near future, very soon. We do not know, however, when this will happen and who will succeed him. From the beginning of the pre-trial proceedings, Your Honour, until today, Mr. Balijagic has been the only, and I repeat it, the only Defence counsel for the accused. According to himself, he only since for a very short period of time has an assistant, we just heard, since three to four days. He never had and he still doesn't have a Defence co-counsel. If he would withdraw in near future, meaning only a few months before the Defence is supposed to file its pre-trial brief, it can be anticipated that a successor, whoever it may be, will not be in a position to familiarise him or herself with the complex factual basis of this case and the even more complex legal issues involved in the present case, whose knowledge are crucial for any substantial defence of the accused. The new Defence counsel, the new lead Defence counsel, would have to go through more than 100 witness statements that form part of the supporting materials. He or she would have to familiarise him or herself with a significant number of documents that form part of the supporting materials. He or she, furthermore, would have to read not only the additional material the Prosecution disclosed in fulfilling its disclosure obligations but also a significant amount of material, hundreds of pages, mainly in B/C/S, that Mr. Balijagic, in support of the defence of his client, provided to the Prosecution a few weeks ago. In addition, any new Defence counsel, he or she would have to develop his own or her own Defence strategy. This Defence strategy, Your Honour, may be very, very different from the Defence strategy of the current Defence counsel. He or she eventually would have to file a Defence pre-trial brief and to file it not later than 31st of July 2002. That's the situation in a nutshell, Your Honour. A reasonable new Defence counsel, even the very best one, Your Honour, would not be able to do all this with the diligence that is necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Whitopf, I'm sorry to interrupt you, but having heard from Mr. Balijagic that he would not resign as counsel, can you move on to another topic?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Yes. I want to stress that the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I can get back to the counsel issue later.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: No, only one sentence. The information we got from Mr. Balijagic is each time confusing. The one time he says he will get an assistant, the one time he says he will get a co-counsel, the next time he says he will withdraw, the next time he says he will not withdraw. That's the situation we have to address and you have, as the Pre-Trial Judge in this matter, you have to take in consideration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But having heard that, does it have anything that has something to do with the timing for the Prosecution to file a pre-trial brief?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: It has something to do, otherwise I wouldn't have it outlined to such an extent. It definitely means a delay, a delay caused by the Defence, a significant delay caused by the conduct of the Defence side. This delay is caused irrespective of the filing date of the Prosecution's pre-trial brief. Keeping this in mind, it doesn't make any sense to maintain the order that the Prosecution is obliged to file its pre-trial brief by 20 April 2002 since the Defence would never be able to file the response, the Defence pre-trial brief, on 31st of July 2002. But I will move on to the next issue. That's even a more interesting and a more crucial issue. That's the jurisdictional issue. The Defence in the case the Prosecutor versus Hadzihasanovic and others has raised the issue as to whether Article 7 (3) of the Tribunal Statutes is applicable in a situation of a non-international armed conflict, in a non-international armed conflict. The applicability of Article 7(3) in a non-international armed conflict is an issue that plays a role in this matter as well. It is a preliminary issue, Your Honours. As in the Hadzihasanovic and others case, traditional logic requires that the present case -- that we get a decision in the present case or in the Hadzihasanovic and others case on this issue prior to any other movements. The Trial Chamber in Hadzihasanovic, as you already know, has issued a Scheduling Order. The parties in that case have to file final submissions by the end of 2002. Afterwards, the Trial Chamber in Hadzihasanovic and others has to issue its decision. It's obvious that the party's whose submissions will not be granted will appeal. Whatever the decision will be, a binding -- a binding decision by the Appeals Chamber will only be issued late fall this year, maybe even later. That's the second issue, Your Honour. There's a third issue, and unfortunately this issue concerns stipulations. In January, we were very optimistic that Mr. Balijagic and the Prosecution would be able to find some agreements on facts. But unfortunately, this did not happen. We submitted Mr. Balijagic a comprehensive list of facts we would like to get his opinion. We got a response, but it was not a response in a yes or no format. We got a response making comments to certain facts. That's obviously not the format you need for stipulations. The Prosecution submitted another set, a very similar one, on 21st March, and only today we got the answer of the Defence outlining that the accused is not willing and not ready to enter in any discussions with the Prosecution on stipulations. That is a new movement and that to a high extent changes the situation as compared to the situation in January this year. Again, another reason to defer the current deadline of a final pre-trial brief. Let me now address the issue of translations, and I'm sure Your Honour is very familiar with the overall situation on translations. We all know that translations are the bottleneck of all ICTY proceedings. The Prosecution in this matter over the last month did everything possible to significantly narrow down the amount of material that needs to be translated, and I'm sure you are aware of the discussion we had during the Rule 65 ter meetings. We have 1.171 pages to be translated by CLSS, but this is only the material that was provided to us prior to February 2002, prior to the fact that we got a large amount of additional material by both, by the Defence and the Bosnian government in answering a number of Prosecution requests. These documents are ranging in a number of thousands of pages that may have serious impact on the present case, both culpatory and exculpatory nature. The area in particular to be considered are JNA manuals which the accused, in the course of his interview as an accused, in late fall last year provided the Prosecutor with. Translations of these manuals need to be provided to the Prosecution military expert. The Defence military expert, and I want to stress that the Defence military experts are able and are in a position to read the B/C/S material, apparently relied on those materials. The Prosecution cannot address issues raised by the Defence military experts in its pre-trial brief without exactly knowing what the manuals are saying. Although the Prosecution has narrowed down the translation request to the absolute minimum, and I want to repeat to the absolute minimum some 400 pages need to be translated with regard to the JNA manuals. Translation of those manuals need a particular expertise. Last inquiries have revealed that 58 pages are currently translated, and this task will not be finished prior to summer this year. To summarise on this issue also, the Prosecution has done everything, everything possible to narrow down the amount of material to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. be translated. Large amounts of crucial materials, crucial for our final pre-trial brief, still evade translation. Coming to an end now, Your Honour, I want lastly to address the issue of a military expert. I already briefly touched on it. The current situation on the Prosecution side is not the result of a late call by the Prosecution. The Prosecution has made first efforts already in September last year, efforts to identify a suitable military expert, a general whose mother tongue is neither one of the official languages nor B/C/S has been chosen. Members of the trial team met him, met him in October last year, and it turned out that the General was well-qualified as a Prosecution military expert witness. However, after further consideration, the Prosecution decided not to use him. The main reason for that, and I'm sure Your Honour will appreciate this, has been that the General doesn't speak English and that this would cause further delay. A new military expert has now been identified. The team met him a few weeks ago. Significant amounts of materials have been handed over to the military expert. The expert is supposed to come back to us next week to inform us whether he's willing and in a position to assist the Prosecution. After the meeting I just mentioned, a professional schedule has been discussed. We were told by the expert that he would not be able to submit his written expert opinion prior to August 2002 at the earliest. Your Honour, the Prosecution is well aware that it is not obliged to file a or the written military expert opinion with the pre-trial brief. However, the final written expert opinion in a case like the present one may have such significant impact on the contents of the pre-trial brief that the Prosecution is hardly in a position to file its pre-trial brief without the sound opinion of a military expert. To summarise, and now coming to an end, each of the reasons just outlined gives reason enough to defer the filing of the Prosecution's pre-trial brief. The combination of these reasons, in the opinion of the Prosecution, makes it necessary. From the point of view of the Prosecution, end of September, end of September seems to be a realistic deadline to file its final pre-trial brief. Thank you very much, Your Honour, having given me the opportunity to extensively outline the Prosecution's position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have anything to say, Mr. Balijagic, to this?

utterances.speaker: MR. BALIJAGIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I certainly have. Your Honour, I have listened to Mr. Whitopf with great attention indeed, and I must say that in my today's discussions in the Chief Prosecutor's office with Mr. Whitopf, and I must say that we not only have the language barrier between us but it seems to me sometimes that I live on planet Mars. I say this regarding the indictment against my client. That is why I asked the representatives of the OTP to take care of the charges listed in the indictment and the pleadings in the indictment, not worry about the defence of my client. I said that on our part, we will not be the cause of any delay. And I will repeat here that we are ready to start trial as soon as tomorrow. I want to point out that we have provided the Prosecution already with all the Defence witness statements. In order to facilitate the work of this Court and for the sake of the truth, allow me to add one more thing. I was truly shocked today, at the office of Mr. Whitopf. My client and I understood our cooperation with the Prosecution office, and we have stated so in this court, that this cooperation is to serve the purposes of establishing the truth, and my client even said that he would even be prepared to sign his own conviction. Mr. Whitopf also raised the issue of my client's pronouncing himself guilty. My client will certainly not do that. Last year, I referred the representatives of the Prosecution office to the file of the secret police in Sarajevo, titled "Sefer Halilovic." The existence of this file means that he was the subject of special treatment. Top experts of the secret police, Mustafa Zdravko, the chief of the Yugoslav secret police, said that such a man could not command a group of people let alone a wide military operation. We have also provided the OTP with numerous military expertise, all with a view of facilitating the work of this Court and establishing the truth on the crimes committed. For all these reasons, I believe that it is extremely incorrect and unfair on behalf of the Prosecution to conclude that we will be late with our pre-trial brief, which was scheduled to be filed before the 31st of July, the last Status Conference of the 8th of January. We are expecting the Prosecution's pre-trial brief, and we will be immediately ready to respond to it. And there is one more thing. Our witnesses were taken as samples, and we have already heard, talked to 30 very high-quality witnesses, but we are ready to call 500 more witnesses to help establish the truth, and we are ready to provide the Court and the OTP with their statements, if necessary. I would therefore like you to accept if I say that there is absolutely no need to defer the filing of this pre-trial brief, and I am ready, on the instructions of my client, to start this trial as urgently as possible because this indictment, pleaded as it is, is a great burden to him. And I regret that you are unduly burdened by this issue of the Defence of Mr. Halilovic. And that would be all I have to say. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Before getting to the individual issues raised by the Prosecution's motions, I'd like to stress at this moment that the -- before that, I noticed that the Prosecution seems to emphasise that, by this extension of time, the actual commencement of the trial will not be delayed, but I'd like to stress that the -- whether the actual commencement date will be delayed or not is not a real issue. It seems to me that the Chamber of this Tribunal, before I arrived here, has made it a principle to have cases get ready for trial as soon as possible, that is in six months after the indictment. The reason being is this: As you know, since this Trial Chamber is tied up with Mr. Milosevic's trial for the moment, and which is expected to last certainly more than a year from now, and thus this case might not possibly be heard until the end of that case. But however, we cannot exclude the possibility that the current Milosevic trial could be adjourned for an extensive period of time for any reason or that there might be another possibility of a couple of cases being heard at the same time in parallel. But in such cases, suppose there's no case in this Trial Chamber ready for trial. Then it will be very frustrating. So it is our aim to make cases get ready as soon as possible, irrespective of the actual commencement of the trial. And that's the underlying position of the Trial Chamber, and I will deal -- let's deal with these individual issues. When was this case indicted? This seems a quite recent one. September 2001. It's a quite recent indictment compared to other cases. So my guess is that the Prosecution should have a fresh memory than any other case, which means that there will be no great difficulty for the Prosecution to produce a pre-trial brief. So I'd like to hear why do you need to assess the newly obtained materials? And do you think it will -- the outcome of the assessment of the newly obtained materials or the military expert report will affect the basic structure of the indictment greatly?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I refer to the military expert side in that's our main concern. This is a 7.3 case, command responsibility under Article 7(3). We got six military expert reports from the Defence side addressing a variety of issues that are crucial for this matter. To respond to these issues, we need to have the JNA manuals fully translated. I outlined the current situation with regard to this issue. We will only be in a position to respond, to respond in a pre-trial brief to these crucial issues as soon as we have the JNA manuals translated. That takes time. The military expert, the Prosecution military expert will need sufficient time to provide his expert opinion, and that's the main reason we would like to file a final pre-trial brief at a later stage, and as I already mentioned, September 2002 would be a very realistic time frame. Another solution would be that we file a provisional pre-trial brief as it has been granted in a variety of other cases, and we would file a final pre-trial brief later on. Again, September would be a realistic time frame.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The reluctance for the Court to accept the word "provisional" is that -- it's my personal feeling that the word "provisional" seems to make the work of the -- whoever it is, the brief lacking some kind of sincerity. So what I want is a final brief. The word "final" meaning the best brief you can produce at this moment. And that does not necessarily prevent the parties or necessarily prevent the pre-trial brief supplemented to or added to later on. So you can agree to this?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: On principle, I would agree with you, Your Honour. However, there are further considerations I have to make. First of all, provisional pre-trial briefs have been granted in a number of ICTY cases. They have been granted in Galic. They have been granted in Ademi. They have been granted in Krajisnik and Plavsic and they have recently been granted in Stakic, and I think all cases should be treated similar. An even more crucial issue is the fact that we have to include exhibits, list of exhibits -- add a list of exhibits to our pre-trial brief, our final pre-trial brief. This is a quite difficult exercise since currently we would be able to include 156 exhibits, but as I already announced, as I already informed you about, we have to wait for translations, and we can anticipate that for our final pre-trial brief in September we would thoroughly be able to refer to around 500 exhibits. That's another reason why we would like to file our final pre-trial brief at a later stage. Finally, it will finally serve the acceleration of the trial itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BALIJAGIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may. Just a word.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Balijagic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BALIJAGIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have reached an agreement today with representatives of the OTP and I would like to have it on record. The file of Sefer Halilovic containing 3.250 pages belongs in the category of material whose discovery or disclosure leads to the acquittal of the accused. The file of the terrorist group Seve who committed a terrorist act against my client Sefer Halilovic -- will you allow me to finish, please, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you make it very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BALIJAGIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish this to be entered in the record, namely, my request that this material be made available to the Defence as exculpatory material. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it that you are triggering the Rule 66(B) disclosure, if I understand it correctly?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I first strictly oppose any attempt by the Defence counsel to enter into a discussion on the merits of this case. That's what he tried to do right now. Secondly, you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. That's what I was going to point out later. Yes. Next point.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: You are quite rightly addressing the subject of reciprocal disclosure and that is a subject has been confused on the Defence side all the time. Mr. Balijagic, as the Defence counsel for the accused, submits a high amount of material to the Prosecution. That would mean he is actually doing what he would be requested under Rule 67(C) if he would have triggered reciprocal disclosure. However, the Prosecution asked him several times does he explicitly trigger reciprocal disclosure. We never, never ever got a clear answer. We are currently working under our disclosure obligations. We consider them Rule 66(A)(i)-(ii), Rule 68. There is no explicit either verbal nor written announcement that reciprocal disclosure has been triggered, and I would like to have it on the record what is the situation on the Defence side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Coming back to the issues, the issues relating to the military expert report and some translations of newly obtained materials. In my opinion, those circumstances, they will cause a delay in producing a pre-trial brief. You like to call it a provisional pre-trial brief but with the possibility that the pre-trial brief can be supplemented to. I would like you to produce a pre-trial brief as soon as possible. So I would not allow an extension of time to file a pre-trial brief for the reasons that are stated above only, but however, there is one thing I have in mind, I'm really concerned about. It's about stipulations, as you stated. What I heard from the Senior Legal Officer is that the parties are very cooperative, but I notice it's quite different today. So has there been any progress? I'd like to hear from -- having heard from the Prosecution, I'd like to hear from Mr. Balijagic about the stipulations or agreed facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. BALIJAGIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it is true that we have made maximum efforts to cooperate with the OTP with a view to establishing the truth about crimes in Grabovica and Uzdol. It is true that the Prosecution offered us some incontestable facts. However, after analysing the evidence that is available to the Defence, we responded by describing the situation as it is actually. We had it translated into English. On the 19th of February, together with about 50 documents which haven't been translated, that's true, presented this to the OTP. The Prosecution was not satisfied with our response because our response contains the truth and only the truth which is exculpatory and acquitting for Sefer Halilovic, and they suggested that we draft a new response, replying with a yes or no. When I informed my client, the accused Halilovic, about this, he was very concerned and shocked indeed, and couldn't understand why Mr. Whitopf was ignoring our claims made in the response concerning incontestable facts or stipulated facts. That is why we have to leave it to the Court to decide on the merits. We really have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Balijagic, I'm sorry, I have to interrupt you at this stage. The merit will be decided, will be heard and decided upon later on, after the trial commences. So why don't you at this moment concentrate more on procedural matters and especially at this moment on the stipulations. So you haven't answered to the question of the Prosecution. Could you clarify that? You said you just sent extensive materials to the Prosecution without any response to the questions of the Prosecution. Is it true?

utterances.speaker: MR. BALIJAGIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We responded to the question, Your Honour, but not with a yes or no. We responded in the form of our own version of stipulated facts and suggested that the OTP respond to that and assume the responsibility for their answer, whatever it is, if they failed to verify them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Have you got any answers?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Your Honour, to make it clear, we submitted a first set of potential stipulated facts to the Defence counsel. It was a set comprised of 100, 150 individual facts, facts obviously related to the indictment. The concept of stipulations only allows to answer by a yes or no. It's not designed to make comments to these facts. Unfortunately, Mr. Balijagic made comments and altered these facts. We didn't appreciate Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. it. We submitted a second set of potential stipulated facts to Mr. Balijagic. It was a very similar set. And today, just a few hours ago, we got an answer, we got an answer by Mr. Balijagic, saying that his client is not willing to enter in stipulations. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So the Defence will not enter into stipulations to sort out the agreed facts or facts not disputed in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BALIJAGIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, Your Honour. Look, if you will allow me to just briefly describe one thing. I'll take five witnesses who testified before the cantonal court in Sarajevo, and they said my client was [as interpreted] a commander. The same five people testified before the Prosecution and said that he was a commander. So their statements are contradictory. And we cannot agree about this. That's why we failed to reply with a yes or no. We just described things as they really were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It may be that the -- one of the causes which makes the Defence difficult is that the questionnaire itself might be too extensive. I noticed the extensive list of facts. How long was that? You said 150 questions? And the later one consisted of how many?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: I can't give you the exact number, but it should be in the range of at least 100. It was two and a half pages. But they were such simple facts as the date of the independence of Croatia, the date of birth of the accused, such kind of thing. You understand? Such very basic things. We didn't get an answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Balijagic, at this moment let's forget the merit. So do you understand? Whether Mr. Halilovic, your client is innocent or guilty. And having said that, I'd like to ask you whether you can put in writing a brief response to the indictment itself, which consists of one count and two incidents, one in Grabovica and one in Uzdol. So -- among which -- can you sort out facts you can agree to and those you cannot agree to? Is it possible for you?

utterances.speaker: MR. BALIJAGIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we can certainly agree and we have agreed, if I may remind Mr. Prosecutor Whitopf on the place of birth, date of birth, conflict, et cetera, but we cannot agree with facts which are founded in unverifiable and false statements and documents. So we have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Balijagic. Mr. Balijagic. Forget about the evidence. Just concentrate on the indictment itself. You can agree some CVs of your client, Mr. Halilovic was born on some day and blah, blah. You can agree to that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. BALIJAGIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have already agreed to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you go a little further --

utterances.speaker: MR. BALIJAGIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But shall I emphasise? We have already drafted certain corrections for the benefit of the Prosecution regarding the schools he graduated from, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. But -- yes. There's a list in the indictment. Is it municipality -- in Grabovica, the list of some 33 dead persons, people. You -- do you dispute whether these people died at this place at that time or you agree to that kind of facts, for example?

utterances.speaker: MR. BALIJAGIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have agreed on all facts which do not relate to the merits of the case, and we cannot agree on any facts which bear on the merits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you do not agree to these -- for example, Mr. Pero died in Grabovica at this time of day, as written in the indictment? So you cannot agree on any facts regarding merits? Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. BALIJAGIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, how can we agree with that when those things are unfamiliar to us completely? We have learnt about them from the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So the only facts you agree to is the curriculum vitae things of your client? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. BALIJAGIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not only that. There are other things which do not bear on the merits of the case and that we can agree with. But we would like to see a fair draft of these facts or, alternatively, the Prosecution may rely on our set of proposed stipulations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you happen to have the questionnaire with you now? No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BALIJAGIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I have a copy in the Bosnian language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think it will assist me anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution opposes such a procedure. The stipulations is an issue between the parties, and at this point in time, I assume Your Honour shouldn't be involved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Well, it is neither --

utterances.speaker: MR. BALIJAGIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my answers are here as well, showing what was agreed on and everything else. We entered a correction here as to the year when my client attended military academy. We corrected that date. And the second set of questions, I think, had the same number of questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I don't think that will -- I don't think that will assist the Court right now. It is neither the rule nor the practice in this Tribunal to have the response of the Defence at all at this stage, so as such, the Defence is never obliged to make a response to the indictment itself. But in continental -- in countries which adopt the continental legal system, it is very customary to make a brief answer to the indictment. On some parts we agree, yes, like I agree my date of birth and my graduate school, but the others I cannot agree. "I do not know," or something like. Or some part of it. "Yes, I agree that Mr. X died here but it is not from my fault," for example. So I think -- and it's quite -- it may be said that kind of procedure is similar to that of making, producing a stipulation in common law countries. So what I'd like to ask Mr. Balijagic again is that not -- do not respond to the extensive list of facts of the -- from the Prosecution itself but could you sort out the facts which are not disputed by the Defence or accused in the trial among the facts in the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. BALIJAGIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course we shall do that. As far as it does not enter into the merits of the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. Every fact in the indictment itself, without regard any -- any regard to evidence. And with yes, no, and you can put some -- your position in writing. Is it possible?

utterances.speaker: MR. BALIJAGIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, what if I say that Pero Peric was killed, if I agree that he was killed and he is discovered to be alive? Will then there be any consequences --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. You can say what you do not know. Just you don't know. Or -- and these facts -- these kind of facts can be classified as facts the Defence will not argue about it. As such, is it possible?

utterances.speaker: MR. BALIJAGIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But now that we mention this name, I know that two people mentioned in the indictment died of natural causes several years after the event. I know where they were buried. That is why we shall agree only to what we truly consider to be indisputable. But we cannot agree to anything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The purpose of having pre-trial procedure in advance to the actual trial is to help the Court and parties to concentrate on real important issues. For example, in this case, whether Mr. Halilovic bears the command responsibility or not. So we cannot disregard it. We can get over the peripheral things very easily in the trial. So if you can sort out some facts you are not going to argue as early as possible, it will -- the Court and the parties will get on very easily. Certainly you can understand my words.

utterances.speaker: MR. BALIJAGIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I understand you very well. Please give me some time to consult my client. You must understand that he was in a state of shock and anxiety when we received the same set of questions from the Prosecution, with a few exceptions, such as the year of birth, and the Prosecution did not take our comments into account at all. That was a reaction on the part of my client, and of course I have to take instructions from him. But please allow me to discuss the matter with him once again so that we can answer to at least some of these questions with yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. I would say one of the counsel's -- as a professional, one of the counsel's duties is to let his client understand this complicated procedure, so I would appreciate that you can produce some agreed facts with the cooperation of the Prosecution. So in that regard, I would like to give you a month from now. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. BALIJAGIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is very acceptable, Your Honour. We shall do this even sooner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Have a discussion with your client, and please put in writing as detailed as possible. And then after that, the parties can have a 65 ter meeting with our Senior Legal Officer, and then we'll give the Prosecution a month from that to file a pre-trial brief. Does that sound acceptable to the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I understand that means two months from now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: That sounds possible. That sounds acceptable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. I didn't hear about the search programmes, about the search for the witnesses, which -- my impression is -- which really concerns the Prosecution is that the search is not done completely at this moment. Could you make a short comment on that. Witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Your Honour, you know that with regard to disclosure under Rule 66(A)ii), we have to disclose also prior statements of the witnesses we want to call or whose statements we want to use as Rule 92 bis statements. The search has been initiated weeks ago. Unfortunately, due to the Milosevic trial, this search has been blocked for quite a number of weeks. It will only start in the near future. Again only a very little percentage of the witnesses, only the result with regard to a very little percentage of the witnesses has been provided to us. I cannot anticipate at this point in time when these searches will be finished. That is just a matter of reality, and ISO, our search unit, is not in a position to predict how long it will take.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there anything the parties would like to raise at this moment? Yes, Mr. Balijagic?

utterances.speaker: MR. BALIJAGIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence has nothing to raise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are two issues that are still not clear to the Defence. First of all, the announced withdrawal of Mr. Balijagic as Defence counsel, and the second issue is the issue of reciprocal disclosure. We still didn't get an answer to our question whether reciprocal disclosure has been triggered or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Could you clarify this problem, please matters?

utterances.speaker: MR. BALIJAGIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do require reciprocal disclosure. As I have said, the Defence has disclosed everything to the Prosecution, and we ask that the Prosecution do the same, especially as regards material containing exculpatory evidence. By this I'm referring primarily to the two files which I prompted the Prosecution to obtain, and I wish to remind the Prosecution of the Rules of Evidence and Procedure, under which it is their duty to disclose to me any exculpatory evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. And about the first issue? It is certain that you will not resign from this case, will not withdraw from this case?

utterances.speaker: MR. BALIJAGIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, allow me to explain very briefly the reasons for my withdrawal. I am also a victim of genocide, which is punishable under Article 2. In 1994 I fled Sarajevo in an American plane in order not to be assassinated. All the participants of the attack on me are witnesses for the Prosecution. I do not feel comfortable when I see all this. I asked my client to release me, but I was concerned that an appropriate replacement be found for me. I hope that we will find a replacement in Ms. Dijana Kreho or someone else as Defence counsel, and I think I will withdraw. But let me tell you again that all this depends on my client. If my client insists that I remain, I shall listen to the ethics of my profession.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think very appropriate for the Court to ask the client -- the counsel whether it will resign or not any further, so let's take it that he will not resign for the moment. And that will not make any difference to the current position of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Your Honour, with all due respect, I disagree. That will make a difference. Any new Defence counsel will not be in a position to respond to a Prosecution's pre-trial brief within two or there months. That's just not possible if he or she is a reasonable Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That is not the problem of the Prosecution in filing a pre-trial brief. That is what I'm pointing out at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: But you have to consider, with all due respect, that this has some implications. The Defence would get definitely much more time, since any, any new Defence counsel will immediately file a motion for extension of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So that -- but my opinion -- I'm pointing out that will -- cannot be a cause for a Prosecution to delay its pre-trial brief, as you agreed before. And -- yes. Can I see the Senior Legal Officer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Okay. The position of Mr. Balijagic is not quite clear regarding the Rule 66 (B) disclosure, which is reciprocal disclosure. So if you would like to -- if you are saying that you would like to apply for the reciprocal disclosure provided in Rule 66(A)(ii); is that right? 66(B). So could you make it in writing later with some more -- with some clear words? And why don't we leave it as it is. Yes, Mr. Whitopf?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Your Honour, one last observation I have to make. Provided that Mr. Balijagic, the Defence, will invoke reciprocal disclosure, that will have a serious, a crucial impact on our resources. That means that it diminishes our ability to file a pre-trial brief, a final pre-trial brief, within the time frame you just mentioned. And unfortunately, I don't get the impression, I didn't get it during the last conference with the senior legal officer and I didn't get it today that Mr. Balijagic, the Defence, understands, understands the concept of reciprocal disclosure and the impact on the proceedings. I unfortunately have to say this. And Mr. Balijagic must give a clear sign what he wants. Of course we are disclosing Rule 68 material. 68 has nothing to do with 66(B) reciprocal disclosure and I'm not sure that the Defence understands the concept of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. The Prosecution's position has been noted, and I will make it clear if necessary. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. BALIJAGIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have understood your order that I should make my submissions in writing. It is true we raised this issue with Ms. Yvonne Featherstone during one of our meetings when Mr. Ekkehard said that their Sarajevo dossier contained 50.000 pages and that it would slow down the proceedings, delay the trial, and then I asked that only Rule 68 evidence be provided, that is, exculpatory evidence focusing only on the two files of Sefer Halilovic and the Seve terrorist group, but I will certainly make my submissions in writing, Your Honour. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. One thing I forgot is the timetable for the Defence pre-trial brief. You yourself can respond as soon as -- immediately, immediately after the Prosecution's pre-trial brief, but is three months enough for you after the pre-trial brief -- to produce a Defence pre-trial brief?

utterances.speaker: MR. BALIJAGIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Roughly two months from now the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In two months the Prosecution is ordered to file its pre-trial brief, and afterwards, in three months again, the Defence will file its pre-trial brief. Unless there is anything the parties would like to raise at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Your Honour, no further observations from the side of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This hearing is adjourned, and you will have a 65 ter conference after the Defence has produced its brief response to the indictment. And it is very much encouraged to both parties to communicate in producing such a response. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: at 4.22 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: [Trial Chamber and Senior Legal Officer confer]
[Trial Chamber and Senior Legal Officer confer]
[Trial Chamber and Senior Legal Officer confer]
